subject: social_science
chapter_title: The Making of a Global World

concepts.title: The Pre-Modern World
concepts.definition: Before the modern era of nations and formal trade agreements, people across the world were connected through travel, migration, trade and the exchange of ideas, crops, diseases and technologies over long distances.
concepts.key_idea: Global interconnectedness is not a modern phenomenon; long-distance cultural and economic exchanges shaped the pre-modern world.
question_patterns: Explain how the pre-modern world was interconnected.
What role did travellers play in connecting distant regions?
How did the spread of crops and diseases affect societies before 1500?
Why is it incorrect to think of globalisation as a purely recent phenomenon?
Describe the channels through which pre-modern global links operated.

solution_steps.action: Identify the channels of pre-modern connection
solution_steps.explain: List travel, migration, trade, conquest and religious missions as the main channels.

solution_steps.action: Map the exchanges that flowed through these channels
solution_steps.explain: Crops, diseases, technologies, ideas and goods moved across regions.
Assess how these exchanges altered economies, diets and cultures over time.

worked_examples.question: How were people of the pre-modern world connected with one another?
worked_examples.solution: Travellers, traders, migrants and pilgrims moved across regions carrying goods, ideas and technologies. These long-distance exchanges created cultural and economic links well before modern globalisation.
worked_examples.answer: Through travel, trade, migration and the spread of ideas, crops, diseases and technologies.

worked_examples.question: Give one example of a crop that travelled across the world in pre-modern times.
worked_examples.solution: Potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chillies spread from the Americas to Europe and Asia after the sixteenth century, transforming diets globally.
worked_examples.answer: Potatoes / maize / tomatoes / chillies (any one).

exercises.question: Explain the meaning of the 'pre-modern world' in the context of global connections.
List three channels through which pre-modern societies were linked.

concepts.title: Silk Routes Link the World
concepts.definition: Silk routes were a network of overland and maritime trade paths that connected East Asia to the Mediterranean and Europe, carrying silk, goods, culture and religion across vast distances for centuries.
concepts.key_idea: The silk routes were early arteries of global trade and cultural exchange, linking regions through commerce and religion.
question_patterns: What were the silk routes and why were they important?
How did the silk routes promote cultural exchange along with trade?
Name the goods that travelled along the silk routes.
Explain the geographic span of the silk routes.
How did the silk routes link the East and the West?

solution_steps.explain: Identify them as overland and maritime trade networks connecting East Asia to the Mediterranean.

solution_steps.action: Identify what travelled along the routes
solution_steps.explain: Silk, pottery, spices, precious metals, religion and cultural practices moved along them.
They fostered trade and cultural exchange between distant civilisations for centuries.

worked_examples.question: What were the silk routes?
worked_examples.solution: The silk routes were a network of trade paths -- both overland and by sea -- that connected China and East Asia with Central Asia, West Asia and the Mediterranean, carrying silk and many other goods.
worked_examples.answer: Trade networks connecting East Asia to the Mediterranean carrying silk and other goods.

worked_examples.question: How did the silk routes help in the spread of religion?
worked_examples.solution: Buddhist preachers and Christian missionaries travelled along these routes, spreading their faith to new regions.
worked_examples.answer: They enabled the spread of Buddhism and Christianity across regions.

exercises.question: Describe the importance of the silk routes in linking the world.
Name two goods and one religion that travelled along the silk routes.

concepts.title: Food Travels: Spread of New Crops
concepts.definition: The discovery and conquest of the Americas introduced new crops such as potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes to Europe and Asia, dramatically changing global diets and populations.
concepts.key_idea: The movement of new crops from the Americas transformed food habits and supported population growth in Europe and Asia.
question_patterns: How did new crops from the Americas change diets in Europe and Asia?
Explain the role of potatoes in Europe's population growth.
Which crops travelled from the Americas to the rest of the world?
Why was the spread of new crops significant for global history?
How did food travel contribute to global interconnection?

solution_steps.action: Identify the source region of new crops
solution_steps.explain: Recognise the Americas as the origin of potatoes, maize, tomatoes and chillies.

solution_steps.action: Trace the spread of these crops
solution_steps.explain: Follow their movement to Europe and Asia through trade and colonisation.

solution_steps.action: Assess the demographic and dietary impact
solution_steps.explain: Evaluate how new crops improved nutrition and supported population growth.

worked_examples.question: How did potatoes change the lives of the poor in Europe?
worked_examples.solution: Potatoes became a staple food for the poor because they were cheap, nutritious and easy to grow, helping to reduce famine and support population growth.
worked_examples.answer: Potatoes improved nutrition and supported population growth among the poor.

worked_examples.question: Name two crops that travelled from the Americas to India.
worked_examples.solution: Maize and chillies were introduced to India from the Americas and became part of Indian agriculture and cuisine.
worked_examples.answer: Maize and chillies (also tomatoes, potatoes).

exercises.question: Explain how the spread of new crops affected the population of Europe.
List three crops introduced to the Old World from the Americas.

concepts.title: Conquest, Disease and Trade
concepts.definition: European conquest of the Americas was aided by the spread of germs like smallpox, which decimated indigenous populations, while precious metals from the Americas fuelled European trade with Asia.
concepts.key_idea: Disease, conquest and trade were intertwined; germs enabled conquest and silver from the Americas integrated global trade.
question_patterns: How did disease help European conquest of the Americas?
Explain the role of silver in the early modern global economy.
What was the impact of smallpox on the native peoples of the Americas?
How did conquest and trade reinforce each other in this period?
Why did European soldiers not need large armies to conquer the Americas?

solution_steps.explain: Recognise that smallpox and other germs killed large numbers of indigenous people.

solution_steps.action: Trace the flow of precious metals
solution_steps.explain: Silver and gold from the Americas moved to Europe and then to Asia to pay for goods.
Explain how conquest provided the wealth that integrated global markets.

worked_examples.question: Why did the conquest of the Americas not require large European armies?
worked_examples.solution: The native populations had no immunity to European diseases like smallpox, which killed millions and weakened resistance far more effectively than armies.
worked_examples.answer: Diseases like smallpox decimated native populations, reducing the need for large armies.

worked_examples.question: How did silver from the Americas affect global trade?
worked_examples.solution: Silver mined in the Americas flowed to Europe and then to China and India to pay for goods, linking the Americas, Europe and Asia into a single trade network.
worked_examples.answer: Silver from the Americas fuelled global trade by flowing to Asia in exchange for goods.

exercises.question: Explain the connection between conquest, disease and trade in the making of the global world.
How did precious metals from the Americas influence trade with Asia?

concepts.title: A World Economy Takes Shape
concepts.definition: By the nineteenth century, a global economy emerged through trade in goods, labour and capital, supported by colonies, new technologies and the migration of millions of people.
concepts.key_idea: A true world economy took shape in the nineteenth century through trade, migration and capital flows across regions.
question_patterns: Describe the main features of the nineteenth-century world economy.
How did migration contribute to the global economy?
What role did colonies play in the world economy?
Explain how trade, migration and capital were linked in this period.
Why is the nineteenth century seen as the period when a world economy took shape?

solution_steps.action: Identify the three flows of the global economy
solution_steps.explain: Recognise the flows of goods, labour and capital across regions.
Colonies supplied raw materials, markets and labour for the world economy.
Millions migrated for work, linking distant economies through labour.

worked_examples.question: What were the three types of flows that shaped the global economy in the nineteenth century?
worked_examples.solution: The three flows were the trade in goods (e.g., cloth and wheat), the flow of labour (migration), and the movement of capital for investment.
worked_examples.answer: Trade in goods, flow of labour, and movement of capital.

worked_examples.question: Why did nearly 50 million people emigrate from Europe in the nineteenth century?
worked_examples.solution: Poverty, hunger and the demand for labour in colonies and the Americas pushed millions of Europeans to migrate in search of work and a better life.
worked_examples.answer: Poverty and the demand for labour drove large-scale European migration.

exercises.question: Describe how a world economy took shape in the nineteenth century.
Name the three flows that linked the global economy.

concepts.title: Role of Technology
concepts.definition: Technological advances such as railways, steamships, the telegraph and the Suez Canal transformed transportation and communication, making global trade faster and cheaper.
concepts.key_idea: Technology shrank the world by reducing the time and cost of trade and communication, enabling closer global integration.
question_patterns: How did technology transform global trade in the nineteenth century?
Explain the significance of the Suez Canal.
What role did railways and steamships play in the world economy?
How did the telegraph affect global communication?
Why was technology crucial for the making of a global world?

solution_steps.explain: List railways, steamships, telegraph and the Suez Canal as major innovations.
They reduced transport costs and time, expanding trade volumes.

solution_steps.action: Assess the effect on global integration
solution_steps.explain: Faster trade and communication linked distant markets more tightly.

worked_examples.question: How did the Suez Canal help global trade?
worked_examples.solution: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, reduced the distance between India and Europe by about 6,000 km, making trade faster and cheaper.
worked_examples.answer: It shortened the route between India and Europe, reducing distance by about 6,000 km.

worked_examples.question: How did railways and steamships affect the transport of goods?
worked_examples.solution: They allowed goods to be transported much faster and in larger quantities, lowering costs and connecting inland regions to ports.
worked_examples.answer: They made transport faster, cheaper and higher-capacity.

exercises.question: Explain the role of technology in the making of a global world.
State one way the Suez Canal reduced trade costs.

concepts.title: Late Nineteenth-Century Colonialism
concepts.definition: In the late nineteenth century, European powers expanded colonial control over Africa and Asia, restructuring local economies to supply raw materials and food for the growing world economy.
concepts.key_idea: Colonial expansion reorganised economies in Africa and Asia to serve the needs of the industrial world economy.
question_patterns: How did late nineteenth-century colonialism reshape local economies?
Explain the transformation of agriculture in colonies.
What was the 'scramble for Africa' and why did it matter?
How did colonial powers use colonies in the global economy?
Why did colonialism intensify in the late nineteenth century?

solution_steps.explain: Recognise Africa and parts of Asia as targets of European expansion.
Colonies were made to grow cash crops and export raw materials and food.
Local economies became dependent on exports and were integrated into the world economy.

worked_examples.question: How was West Africa transformed by colonial trade in the late nineteenth century?
worked_examples.solution: Britain and France encouraged cultivation of crops like cocoa and cotton in West Africa, turning it into an exporter of raw materials for the world economy.
worked_examples.answer: West Africa was reorganised to export cash crops like cocoa and cotton.

worked_examples.question: What was the 'scramble for Africa'?
worked_examples.solution: In the 1880s, European powers rapidly divided and colonised Africa to control its resources and markets, redrawing its political map.
worked_examples.answer: The rapid colonisation and division of Africa by European powers in the 1880s.

exercises.question: Describe how late nineteenth-century colonialism changed the economies of colonies.
Name two cash crops promoted in the colonies.

concepts.title: The Inter-War Economy
concepts.definition: The First World War caused massive destruction and debt; the post-war period saw economic instability, the Great Depression of 1929, and the collapse of the first phase of globalisation.
concepts.key_idea: War, debt and the Great Depression disrupted the interconnected world economy built in the nineteenth century.
question_patterns: How did the First World War affect the world economy?
Explain the causes and effects of the Great Depression of 1929.
Why did the gold standard collapse?
How did the inter-war period affect global trade?
What were the economic consequences of the war for Britain and Europe?

solution_steps.explain: Recognise war debt, reparations and the Great Depression as key shocks.
Unemployment, falling prices and reduced trade followed the Depression.
The first phase of globalisation collapsed as trade barriers rose.

worked_examples.question: How did the First World War affect Britain's economy?
worked_examples.solution: Britain borrowed heavily from the USA to finance the war, shifting world financial leadership from London to New York and leaving Britain with huge debts.
worked_examples.answer: Britain fell into debt and financial leadership shifted to New York.

worked_examples.question: What was the Great Depression of 1929?
worked_examples.solution: It was a severe worldwide economic collapse triggered by the fall of the US stock market, leading to unemployment, falling agricultural prices and reduced trade.
worked_examples.answer: A global economic collapse starting in 1929 with unemployment and falling prices.

exercises.question: Explain the impact of the Great Depression on the world economy.
How did the First World War change the financial position of Britain?

concepts.title: Bretton Woods Institutions
concepts.section: Rebuilding a World Economy: The Post-War Era
concepts.definition: The 1944 Bretton Woods Conference established the IMF and the World Bank to stabilise currencies and finance post-war reconstruction, creating a framework for the post-war global economy.
concepts.key_idea: The Bretton Woods system created institutions to manage currency stability and development finance, shaping the post-war economy.
question_patterns: What was the Bretton Woods agreement and why was it important?
Explain the roles of the IMF and the World Bank.
How did Bretton Woods aim to avoid economic instability?
What problems did the Bretton Woods system try to solve?
How did the Bretton Woods system link national economies?

solution_steps.explain: Recognise the IMF and the World Bank as the key outcomes of Bretton Woods.
The IMF stabilised exchange rates; the World Bank financed reconstruction and development.
The framework aimed to prevent the instability of the inter-war years.

worked_examples.question: What were the two main institutions set up at Bretton Woods?
worked_examples.solution: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (World Bank) were established in 1944.
worked_examples.answer: The IMF and the World Bank.

worked_examples.question: What was the main goal of the Bretton Woods system?
worked_examples.solution: It aimed to preserve economic stability and full employment by linking national currencies to the US dollar and creating institutions to manage the global economy.
worked_examples.answer: To ensure economic stability and full employment through coordinated institutions.

exercises.question: Describe the purpose and outcomes of the Bretton Woods Conference.
State one function of the IMF and one of the World Bank.

concepts.title: Decolonisation and Globalisation
concepts.section: Rebuilding a World Economy: The Post-War Era
concepts.definition: After 1945, decolonisation created new nations in Asia and Africa, while from the 1970s onwards the Bretton Woods system weakened and a new phase of globalisation emerged through trade, finance and multinational corporations.
concepts.key_idea: Decolonisation and the later shift to flexible exchange rates and global finance marked a new phase of globalisation.
question_patterns: How did decolonisation affect the global economy?
Explain the changes in the global economy from the 1970s.
What was the role of multinational corporations in globalisation?
How did the end of the Bretton Woods system change global finance?
Describe the main features of the late twentieth-century globalisation.

solution_steps.explain: New nations in Asia and Africa reshaped the global political economy.
Fixed exchange rates ended and capital flows and trade expanded rapidly.
Multinational corporations spread production and finance across borders.

worked_examples.question: How did the world economy change after the 1970s?
worked_examples.solution: The Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates broke down, financial markets were deregulated, and multinational corporations expanded global production and trade.
worked_examples.answer: Shift to flexible exchange rates, deregulated finance and MNC-led globalisation.

worked_examples.question: What role did multinational corporations play in the new globalisation?
worked_examples.solution: MNCs spread their production, labour and finance across countries, linking national economies more tightly into global networks.
worked_examples.answer: MNCs integrated production and finance across countries.

exercises.question: Explain how decolonisation and the changes from the 1970s shaped a new phase of globalisation.
Name two features of late twentieth-century globalisation.
